answer:
1. The animation shows a historical comparison of buying and renting in the US. It uses home price data (FHFA), rent data (BLS) and mortgage rates (Freddie Mac). A grid of tiles stands for many possible starting months. Light tiles mean the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark tiles mean the renter was ahead. The labels say "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. The dark band of "renter ahead" tiles changes position and width from frame to frame. It moves across the grid, and a dark column appears on the left edge. The "January 1991" label stays the same in every frame, so I can't tell what the movement tracks. It could be a sweep through start dates or a different holding period. In the last two frames a caption appears: "held five years: buyer ahead in 74.4%". The grid has far more light tiles than dark ones.

3. In most of the historical windows shown, the buyer came out ahead. The caption puts the figure at about 74%, or roughly three out of four, for a five-year hold. The renter came out ahead in a minority of windows, shown as the dark band. The result depends on when someone bought and how long they held, and it describes the past only.

4. The animation doesn't give direct advice. A viewer might take away that buying has usually beaten renting over multi-year holds, and that holding longer helps. They might also take away that buying is not a sure win, because the dark band shows that some periods favored renting.

5. The animation only suggests this through its picture and its "buyer ahead in 74.4%" caption. It never tells the viewer to buy or rent, and its "history, not a forecast" label warns against reading it as advice. Any advice beyond that is my own conclusion.
